posts.author: Jem
posts.content_md:
Hi

I'm very new to holography and find it a fascinating subject. I have so far made (with reasonable success) a couple of simple Denisyuk holograms. I'm currently in the process of getting everything together to enable me to do some split beam work. I guess i've now got well 

and truly hooked and am finding my new hobby immensly interesting - and expensive! 

I work in Optics (Ophthalmic) and was thinking (always a very dangerous 

thing )...

Would it be possible to create a Holographic lens that could be used to 

correct vision? This would be very useful for people who had to wear very high powered lenses as they could be made very thin. I realise durability could be an issue, but i'm sure that could be overcome possibly by some form of laminating/coating etc.

I've tried searching the net but there doesn't appear to be any real 

information on this subject. I posted this query onto alt.lasers and then though that I would probably be better off asking this question on a forum specific to holography.

Perhaps someone could explain to me whether or not this is possible and if not why not? As I mentioned, i'm very new to holography and am just beginning what could turn out to be a rather large learning curve, But, I am willing to listen and learn - curiosity and the thirst for knowledge can be very addictive !

Many thanks for your help in advance.

Cheers

Jem

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
The big problem in using any Holographic Optical Elements is the dispersion; all the different colors of the spectrum will form their own separate images of different sizes and locations. So looking at the real through any "holographic lenses" will be more like viewing fireworks!

Many years ago 3-M attempted to bring to the opthalmic marketplace "bifocal" contact lenses. One focal length was formed by the refraction by the plastic lens in the conventional manner, and the other was formed by a holographic zone plate. The brightness of the images were controlled so they were about equal. The images themselves were superimposed on top of each other, and it was thought that accomodation by the eye would switch from one to the other.

I remember that they were seeking FDA approval, but I have never seen a sample of one of these in real life. If anyone knows more about the fate of this holographic product, please chime in. After having a pair of contacts dry out on my eyeballs and abrade both corneas simultaneously (the worst pain I had ever suffered until I passed a kidney stone!) I have not kept up with that type of vision solution technology.

If anyone would like some pdf's of an extremely thorough article written by Suzanne St. Cyr for holosphere about the project I will send them if you get in contact with me via this forum.
